presidents.name: Ulysses S. Grant
presidents.summary: Grant signed the Enforcement Acts of 1870 and 1871 and used federal troops, martial law, and a suspension of habeas corpus in nine South Carolina counties to prosecute the Ku Klux Klan. He also signed the Civil Rights Act of March 1, 1875, which the Supreme Court struck down in part eight years later.
presidents.paragraph: Grant took office the year the Fifteenth Amendment went to the states, and he signed it in 1870 calling it, in his words, a measure of grander importance than any other act of its kind in the country's history. Congress then passed what came to be called the Enforcement Acts, starting in 1870, to protect the right to vote, and in April 1871 Grant signed the Ku Klux Klan Act. He didn't leave it on paper. In October 1871 he declared counties in the South Carolina upcountry to be in a state of rebellion, suspended the writ of habeas corpus there, and sent in troops, and by year's end more than 600 men had been detained. Federal prosecutors in South Carolina secured 49 guilty pleas in the November 1871 term and convicted all eighteen men tried for conspiracy in the April term. Grant's last major civil rights act, signed March 1, 1875, guaranteed equal access to inns, public transportation, and places of amusement.

presidents.personalRecord: Before the war, Grant enslaved one man, William Jones, acquired from his father-in-law Frederick Dent while Grant farmed at White Haven (1854–1859). On March 29, 1859, Grant went to the St. Louis Courthouse and wrote out a manumission paper freeing Jones (NPS; Journal of the Civil War Era). The manumission document, in Grant's handwriting, is held by the Missouri Historical Society. Historians dispute how Grant acquired Jones — whether by purchase or as a gift from Dent — and the date is unknown.

presidents.name: Rutherford B. Hayes
presidents.summary: Hayes withdrew federal troops from the South Carolina and Louisiana statehouses in April 1877, ending the last federally backed Republican state governments in the South. He had conditioned withdrawal on Southern Democratic promises to protect Black civil and voting rights, and later recorded in his diary that those promises were not kept.
presidents.paragraph: In his inaugural address on March 5, 1877, Hayes said he would work for a civil policy that would, in his words, forever wipe out the color line in the country's political affairs, and he argued that only local government that recognizes and maintains the rights of all is true self-government. Within weeks he did the thing that defines his record. On April 10, 1877, troops left the statehouse in South Carolina after a White House meeting with Daniel Chamberlain and Wade Hampton; Chamberlain gave in and Hampton took office the next day. On April 24 Hayes withdrew soldiers from Louisiana, and Governor Packard submitted. Hayes had asked for pledges that Black Southerners' civil and voting rights would be protected. They weren't. He complained in his diary about violence of the most atrocious character in the 1878 elections. Over the following two decades Black Southerners were disfranchised through poll taxes, literacy tests, intimidation, and violence until virtually none could vote.

presidents.name: James A. Garfield
presidents.summary: In his March 4, 1881 inaugural address Garfield called the elevation of Black Americans from slavery to full citizenship the most important political change since 1787 and said violating the freedom of the suffrage is a crime. He was shot on July 2, 1881 and died that September, about 100 days into a term that produced no civil rights legislation.
presidents.paragraph: Garfield's presidency is almost entirely one speech. On March 4, 1881, in his inaugural address, he said the elevation of the negro race from slavery to the full rights of citizenship is the most important political change the country has known since the adoption of the Constitution of 1787. He went further on voting: bad local government is a great evil, he said, but to violate the freedom and sanctities of the suffrage is more than an evil, it is a crime which, if persisted in, will destroy the Government itself. He tied that to schooling, warning that the census had already sounded the alarm in the appalling figures marking how dangerously high the tide of illiteracy had risen among voters and their children. Then his term ran out. He was struck down by an assassin's bullet just one hundred days after his inauguration, and his domestic agenda, on this and everything else, went unimplemented.

presidents.name: Chester A. Arthur
presidents.summary: The Supreme Court struck down the core of the Civil Rights Act of 1875 in the Civil Rights Cases on October 15, 1883, during Arthur's term. In his annual message of December 4, 1883, Arthur told Congress he would give unhesitating approval to any lawful legislation replacing the invalidated protections; none passed.
presidents.paragraph: On October 15, 1883, the Supreme Court held in the Civil Rights Cases that the first and second sections of the Civil Rights Act of March 1, 1875 were unconstitutional as applied to the states, since the Fourteenth Amendment reaches state action and not private conduct. Justice Harlan dissented, writing that the Court adjudges, he thought erroneously, that Congress lacks power under either the Thirteenth or Fourteenth Amendment to establish such regulations. Arthur responded in his third annual message on December 4, 1883. He noted that certain statutory provisions intended to secure the enforcement of those rights had been recently declared unconstitutional, and said any legislation whereby Congress may lawfully supplement the constitutional guaranties of equal enjoyment of every right and privilege of citizenship would receive his unhesitating approval. Congress passed nothing. Meanwhile in Virginia, the Readjuster coalition that Black voters helped build sent William Mahone to the Senate in 1881, where he caucused with Republicans and dispensed patronage until Democrats broke the coalition after the 1883 Danville violence.

presidents.name: Grover Cleveland
presidents.summary: Cleveland, the only president elected to non-consecutive terms, courted white Southern Democrats and, per the Miller Center, saw African Americans as inferior and opposed integrated schools in New York. During his second term the Democratic 53rd Congress repealed the remaining federal elections protections in 1894.
presidents.paragraph: Cleveland is the one president counted twice, elected in 1884 and again in 1892. On race, the Miller Center's account is blunt: he agreed with white Southerners in their reluctance to treat African Americans as social and political equals, made special efforts to reach out to Democrats and former Confederates in the South to assure them they had a friend in the White House, opposed integrated schools in New York, and saw African Americans as essentially inferior. He did make a few Black appointments. On March 11, 1887 he commissioned Charles Henry James Taylor as minister resident and consul general to Liberia during a Senate recess; Taylor presented credentials June 4 and left the post soon after September 22 that year. Cleveland also gave James C. Matthews a recess appointment as Recorder of Deeds for the District of Columbia, succeeding Frederick Douglass. The larger fact of his second term is that the Democratically controlled 53rd Congress repealed the remaining federal elections protections in 1894.

presidents.name: Benjamin Harrison
presidents.summary: Harrison used his annual messages to press for federal protection of Black voting rights and backed the Lodge federal elections bill introduced June 14, 1890, which passed the House and died in the Senate. In his December 6, 1892 message he told Congress that the frequent lynching of Black Americans was without excuse.
presidents.paragraph: Harrison put the issue in his first annual message on December 3, 1889, saying that in many parts of the country where the colored population is large, people of that race are by various devices deprived of any effective exercise of their political rights, and arguing that the power to take direction of House elections is clearly given to the General Government. He also noted that the colored people did not intrude themselves upon us and had, from a standpoint of ignorance and poverty, made remarkable advances in education and property. The vehicle was Henry Cabot Lodge's federal elections bill, introduced June 14, 1890, which would have let constituents petition a federal judge to take charge of a federal election and let the government appoint supervisors over registration and certification. Southern opponents branded it the Force Bill. It barely passed the House, then languished and died in the Senate over tariff and currency fights. In his message of December 6, 1892, Harrison said the frequent lynching of colored people accused of crime is without excuse.
